content.content:
1	---
2	name: do-task
3	description: |
4	  Does the work a claimed issue describes — writes and commits the change, or performs the
5	  act and captures the evidence that it happened. Holds the scope the issue set, records
6	  why in the commit message rather than only what, and ends by stating what state the work
7	  is actually in rather than declaring it done. The write half of an issue; something else
8	  judges whether it finished.
9	when_to_use: |
10	  Use once an issue is claimed and the work should start, whatever kind it is — "implement
11	  it", "fix it", "make the change", "go ahead", "do it". Code: "write the parser fix".
12	  Docs: "update that README". Environment: "run the staging upgrade". Operations: "rotate
13	  the cert now", "run the migration", "restart it". Reach for it after take-issue has
14	  claimed something, and when the user says do it on work already understood. Not for
15	  choosing what to work on, not for opening a change request, and not for deciding whether
16	  the result is good enough — each of those is somebody else's job.
17	argument-hint: "[issue-number]"
18	---
19	
20	# Take an issue
21	
22	Target: $ARGUMENTS — an issue number, or empty to take the next one available.
23	
24	**This claims, it does not build.** It ends with an issue assigned, a branch cut where one
25	is warranted, and a statement of what was understood. Nothing in the working tree changes,
26	and nothing is acted on — an operation issue is claimed here and performed elsewhere. That gap is
27	deliberate: it is the last cheap moment to catch a misreading, and reading an issue wrong
28	is the failure that survives every later review, because every later review checks the work
29	against the misreading.
30	
31	**It is also the test of the issue.** An issue that cannot be started without asking a
32	question is thin, and here is the only place that is discoverable.
33	
34	**The point is to make the platform pay off.** Every act below is a `gh` or `glab` call a
35	person could make themselves. The value is not having to remember which, not having to
36	notice the two CLIs disagree, and not having to assemble the issue, its comments and its
37	links by hand. Where this skill would add a step the platform does not need, it is wrong —
38	process invented on top of a tracker is a cost the tracker was supposed to remove.
39	
40	## 0. Which platform
41	
42	Derive it — `git remote get-url origin`. Only the verbs this skill needs:
43	
44	| | GitHub — `gh` | GitLab — `glab` |
45	|---|---|---|
46	| read, with comments | `gh issue view <N> --comments` | `glab issue view <N> --comments` |
47	| frontier | `gh issue list --state open --label <ready> --search "no:assignee"` | `glab issue list --label <ready> --output json --jq '[.[] \| select(.assignees\|length==0)]'` |
48	| claim | `gh issue edit <N> --add-assignee @me` | `glab issue update <N> --assignee <username>` |
49	| move state | `gh issue edit <N> --add-label <in-progress> --remove-label <ready>` | `glab issue update <N> --label <in-progress> --unlabel <ready>` |
50	
51	**Unassigned is not a flag on either.** `gh` reaches it through search syntax;
52	`glab` has no unassigned filter at all — `--not-assignee` takes a username, not a blank —
53	so it needs JSON and a filter expression. That asymmetry is why the frontier is worth
54	writing down once rather than improvising per run.
55	
56	**Moving a state means removing the old label, not only adding the new one.** Both CLIs
57	can (`gh --remove-label`, `glab --unlabel`) and it is the easiest half to forget. An issue
58	carrying `ready` and `in-progress` at once keeps coming back in the frontier, so the next
59	run offers work somebody already took.
60	
61	`@me` is documented on `gh issue edit --add-assignee` and on `glab issue list --assignee`.
62	`glab issue update` takes a username, so resolve it rather than assuming the shorthand
63	carries across.
64	
65	## 1. Resolve the portal
66	
67	**Given a number**, that is the portal. Take it even if something else looks more urgent —
68	choosing for the user is not this skill's job.
69	
70	**Given nothing**, run the frontier: open, carrying the project's ready-to-pick-up label,
71	unassigned, and not blocked. First in that set wins.
72	
73	**Blocked-ness is not equally knowable.** GitHub answers it natively. On a free GitLab the
74	blocking relation is a paid feature, so what is reachable is a link that records a relation
75	and gates nothing — read the linked issues and judge it yourself, and say that is what you
76	did. Reporting an unverified frontier as verified is worse than reporting a short one.
77	
78	**Empty frontier is an answer.** Report it and stop. Do not widen the query until something
79	appears; a frontier that had to be relaxed to produce work is not a frontier.
80	
81	## 2. Read it whole
82	
83	Body, every comment, labels, linked issues. Comments are where an issue is amended, and an
84	issue read without them is read at the moment it was filed rather than as it stands.
85	
86	**If the issue links a session log**, read the part it points at. A body has to compress;
87	the log is where the reasoning behind it survives, so it is the cheap way to recover intent
88	the issue could not carry.
89	
90	**Do not open it whole.** It is raw JSONL — one record per line, megabytes of it, most of
91	which is tool output and harness bookkeeping. Reading it end to end spends the context the
92	work needs. Pull out what was said instead:
93	
94	    python3 -c "
95	    import json,sys
96	    for l in open(sys.argv[1]):
97	        d=json.loads(l)
98	        if d.get('type') not in ('user','assistant'): continue
99	        c=(d.get('message') or {}).get('content')
100	        if isinstance(c,str): print(d['type'],':',c[:2000]); continue
101	        for b in (c or []):
102	            if b.get('type')=='text': print(d['type'],':',b['text'][:2000])
103	    " .sessions/<uuid>.jsonl
104	
105	Narrow it further where the issue names a line range or a topic. **Search the log, do not
106	read it** — you are recovering one decision, not reconstructing a session.
107	
108	**A session log is an accuracy aid, not a requirement.** Most issues will not have one, and
109	none of them is unpickable for lacking it. Say it was absent and proceed on what the issue
110	says. Refusing work because a record is missing would make the record more important than
111	the work, which is backwards.
112	
113	## 3. Is it pickable
114	
115	Refuse, and name the gap, when any of these is true:
116	
117	| The issue | Why it is not pickable |
118	|---|---|
119	| has no acceptance line | Nothing says when it is done, so nothing can say it was done wrong |
120	| has an acceptance line nobody else could check | "Quality is acceptable" hands the judgment back to whoever wrote it |
121	| is blocked, and the blocker is open | The work would be redone |
122	| is assigned to someone else | Two people on one issue is worse than nobody. Assigned to **you** is not a refusal — that is resuming, and it is the common case |
123	| describes a symptom with no reproduction, and is a bug | The first act would be inventing one |
124	
125	**Refusing costs one message. Guessing costs the whole change.** A guess made here is
126	invisible afterwards: the branch, the commits and the review all inherit it, and every one
127	of them checks the work against the guess rather than against the need.
128	
129	**Offer the fix, do not just name the gap.** A refusal that ends at "this has no
130	acceptance line" leaves the user with the same problem plus a delay. Propose the line, and
131	on a yes write it to the issue and take it in the same turn — the tracker gets better and
132	the work starts, which is the whole point of standing between a person and the platform.
133	
134	Where it is close, ask rather than refusing. "Done when says the report is clearer —
135	clearer measured how?" is one question and it makes the issue permanently better.
136	
137	## 4. Claim it
138	
139	**First: will this end in a diff?** Not every issue does. Code, docs and
140	infrastructure-as-code produce a patch; an operation — a certificate rotated, a job re-run,
141	data migrated — produces evidence and never touches the tree. The issue's kind usually says
142	which, and its template says how it closes.
143	
144	**No diff, no branch.** A branch with nothing on it is noise, and deleting it later reads as
145	work abandoned. Where it is genuinely unclear, ask — one question is cheaper than a stray
146	branch or a missing one.
147	
148	Then claim it. **Local first, so a failure costs nothing anyone else can see:**
149	
150	    1. branch   ONLY if a diff is coming. issue-<N>-<slug>, cut from the default branch
151	                derived rather than assumed. Where the project declares its own pattern,
152	                that wins. Branch already there? Check it out — resuming is not an error.
153	    2. assign   to yourself
154	    3. label    move the state — new label on, old label off
155	
156	If a later act fails, undo backwards: delete the branch if one was cut, unassign. A
157	half-claim is worse than none — a branch with no assignment reads as unclaimed work, and an
158	assignment with no branch reads as work in progress nobody can find, unless no branch was
159	ever meant to exist. Say which acts landed rather than reporting the claim as whole.
160	
161	## 5. Say what you understood
162	
163	The output is a reading, offered for correction:
164	
165	- what this issue is asking for, in your words rather than its
166	- what "done" means, quoted from the acceptance line
167	- what you will not touch, from Out of scope
168	- where a log exists and disagrees with the issue — **the log wins on reasoning, the issue
169	  wins on scope**. With no log, the issue is the whole of it and nothing is missing
170	
171	Then stop. The next act is somebody's decision, not this skill's.
172	
173	## Steps
174	
175	Copy this checklist and tick each item as you finish it:
176	
177	    Task Progress:
178	    - [ ] Platform derived from the git remote, not assumed
179	    - [ ] Portal resolved — number in hand, or frontier reported empty
180	    - [ ] Issue read whole, comments included
181	    - [ ] Session log read if the issue links one — absent is normal, not a blocker
182	    - [ ] Pickable — or refused, with the gap named
183	    - [ ] Diff coming? decided, and the branch cut only if so
184	    - [ ] Assignee and state label set, old label removed
185	    - [ ] Reading stated, and stopped
186	
187	## Report
188	
189	Two lines and a question:
190	
191	    TAKEN — #42, on issue-42-report-wall. Done when: a report reads in under 30 seconds.
192	    Next: implement it.
193	    Run it, or see what I understood?
194	
195	A refusal is a verdict and reads the same way:
196	
197	    NOT PICKABLE — #51 has no acceptance line; nothing says when it is done.
198	    Next: add one to #51, then take it again.
199	
200	The reading, the frontier query and the session excerpt are prepared and held until asked.
201	
202	# Plan the work
203	
204	Target: $ARGUMENTS — the issue to split, or the work just discussed.
205	
206	**Most work should not be split.** An issue with five steps is one issue. Splitting is for
207	work that holds more than one *deliverable* — pieces that ship separately, get reviewed
208	separately, or could be done by different people at the same time. Splitting anything else
209	buys ceremony and pays in issues nobody closes.
210	
211	**The platform already groups things.** Epics, milestones, iterations, project boards — they
212	exist, they have views the team already reads, and a hand-rolled parent issue with child
213	links drifts from whatever the board actually says. Use what is there.
214	
215	## 0. What this platform can actually do
216	
217	Derive the host — `git remote get-url origin` — then note that **neither CLI gives a
218	complete decomposition primitive.** Check before promising a structure:
219	
220	| | GitHub — `gh` | GitLab — `glab` |
221	|---|---|---|
222	| create a grouping | `gh project create` · milestone via `gh api` | `glab milestone create` |
223	| attach an issue | `gh issue create -m <milestone> -p <project>` | `glab issue create --milestone <m> --epic <id>` |
224	| parent / child | sub-issues via `gh api` only — no first-class verb | epic only, and epics are a **paid tier** |
225	| sprint | a Project iteration field | `glab iteration` is **read-only** |
226	| weak fallback | — | `--linked-issues` — records a relation, gates nothing |
227	
228	**Say what you got.** On a free GitLab there is no epic to attach to and no CLI to make one;
229	the reachable grouping is a milestone. Reporting a milestone as an epic, or a relation as a
230	dependency, promises structure the platform will not keep.
231	
232	## 1. Should this be split at all
233	
234	**Split when** the pieces are independently deliverable — each could be reviewed, merged, or
235	performed without the others, and each is worth doing even if the rest is dropped.
236	
237	**Do not split when:**
238	
239	- The steps are sequential parts of one deliverable. A migration with five steps ships once.
240	- One piece is real work and the rest is under an hour. File the small ones or fold them in.
241	- The split is by *layer* rather than by outcome — "the backend part" and "the frontend
242	  part" of one feature usually ship together and reviewing them apart helps nobody.
243	- Nobody will work on the pieces in parallel. Then the split is bookkeeping.
244	
245	**The test:** could someone close one child and leave the others open, and would the board
246	still make sense? If not, it is one issue.
247	
248	## 2. Find what the project already uses
249	
250	Look before proposing. `gh project list` / `glab milestone list` show what exists, and the
251	issues already carry the answer — an open milestone with issues on it is the project's
252	grouping whatever anyone says.
253	
254	**Where the project uses nothing**, ask rather than choosing. Introducing a board is a
255	decision about how a team works, and it is not this unit's to make. A flat set of issues
256	with no grouping is a legitimate answer and often the right one.
257	
258	## 3. Write the children
259	
260	**File each child rather than writing it here.** A child is a full issue and gets the same
261	treatment as any other: the kind decided, the matching template filled, the duplicate search
262	run, an acceptance line a stranger could check. Reimplementing that inside this unit
263	produces five thinner issues than the same work filed one at a time, which is the opposite
264	of what a split is for.
265	
266	- **One deliverable each.** If a child needs its own children, the split was at the wrong
267	  level.
268	- **Its kind picks its template**, and the children need not share one. A feature may split
269	  into code, a doc, and an operation to run afterwards — three kinds, three templates,
270	  three different acceptance tests.
271	- **Ordering is a fact, not a wish.** Where one child genuinely cannot start until another
272	  finishes, record it with whatever the platform offers, and say what that actually
273	  enforces — see step 0.
274	- **Every child links the parent's session log**, where one exists. The reasoning behind
275	  the split is exactly what a body compresses away, and a child picked up next week starts
276	  cold without it. One link, not a copy.
277	- **The parent keeps the why.** Children carry their own scope and acceptance; the reasoning
278	  that led to this split stays in one place rather than being copied five times.
279	
280	## 4. Attach and report
281	
282	Create the grouping if the project has one and it does not exist yet, attach every child,
283	and leave the parent issue pointing at them.
284	
285	**Do not leave a half-plan.** Five children created and two attached is worse than none —
286	the board shows a structure that is not there. If attachment fails partway, say which
287	landed.
288	
289	## Steps
290	
291	Copy this checklist and tick each item as you finish it:
292	
293	    Task Progress:
294	    - [ ] Platform derived, and its actual grouping support checked
295	    - [ ] Splitting justified — pieces are independently deliverable
296	    - [ ] Existing grouping found, or asked for; none is a valid answer
297	    - [ ] Children written as full issues, each with one deliverable
298	    - [ ] Ordering recorded, and what it enforces stated honestly
299	    - [ ] Every child attached, or the partial state reported
300	
301	## Report
302	
303	Two lines and a question:
304	
305	    SPLIT — #47 into #48, #49, #50 on milestone "parser rewrite". #49 waits on #48.
306	    Next: take #48 — the other two are blocked until it lands.
307	    Run it, or see the children?
308	
309	Declining to split is the more common outcome and reads the same:
310	
311	    NOT SPLIT — #47 is five steps of one migration; it ships once.
312	    Next: take #47 as it stands.
313	
314	Where the platform could not carry the structure, that belongs in the first line:
315	
316	    SPLIT — #47 into #48, #49, #50 on milestone "parser rewrite". No epic: this
317	    instance has none, and the ordering is a relation that gates nothing.
318	    Next: take #48, and do not rely on the platform to stop #49 starting early.
319	
320	The children, the grouping, and the trace are prepared and held until asked.
321	
322	# Do the task
323	
324	Target: $ARGUMENTS — the claimed issue, or the one just picked up.
325	
326	**This writes; it does not judge.** It ends with a commit or a captured act, and a plain
327	statement of what state the work is in. Deciding whether that state is *done* belongs to
328	the pass after this one — an author grading their own work grades it done, which is why the
329	grading is somebody else's.
330	
331	**Two modes, and the issue already says which.** Work ending in a diff writes files and
332	commits them. Work ending in evidence performs an act and records that it happened. A
333	certificate rotation produces no patch; the record of the commands and their output is the
334	only proof it occurred.
335	
336	## 0. Which platform
337	
338	Derive it — `git remote get-url origin`. Only the verbs this skill needs:
339	
340	| | GitHub — `gh` | GitLab — `glab` |
341	|---|---|---|
342	| comment | `gh issue comment <N> --body "…"` | `glab issue note <N> -m "…"` |
343	| close with evidence | `gh issue close <N> --comment "…"` | **two commands** — `glab issue note <N> -m "…"` then `glab issue close <N>` |
344	
345	**`glab issue close` takes no comment.** Note first, close second. Reversed, a failed note
346	leaves a closed issue with no record of what was done — and a closed issue is the one nobody
347	looks at again.
348	
349	## 1. Know what you are doing
350	
351	Read the claim before touching anything: the issue, its comments, the reading `take-issue`
352	stated, and the branch — or the absence of one, which means this ends in evidence.
353	
354	**No claim to read?** "Just fix it" is what people actually type, and it arrives with no
355	assignee, no stated reading, and often no issue. That is workable, not an error — say which
356	you have and carry on:
357	
358	| What is missing | What to do |
359	|---|---|
360	| the branch | Decide the mode yourself: does this end in a diff or in evidence? |
361	| the stated reading | Read the issue and state your own before starting. It is the cheap moment |
362	| the issue itself | Do the work if it is small. If it is not, say so — untracked work of any size is invisible the moment this session ends |
363	
364	Never invent a claim. Reporting an issue as claimed when nothing on the platform says so is
365	worse than working without one.
366	
367	**Three sources, three authorities.** They disagree more often than anyone expects:
368	
369	| Source | Binds on |
370	|---|---|
371	| the code | **reality** — what is true now, whatever anything says |
372	| the issue | **scope** — what this change may touch |
373	| the log | **nothing.** It informs |
374	
375	A log that seems to forbid something is not a constraint; it is a previous person's
376	situation, recorded under conditions that may no longer hold. Where the issue and the code
377	disagree about what exists, the code is right and the issue needs a comment.
378	
379	## 2. Hold the scope
380	
381	**`Out of scope` is binding.** It is the one section written specifically to stop the next
382	person widening the work, and that next person is now you.
383	
384	Finding something else worth doing is normal and is not permission. File it, or say it in
385	the report, and carry on with what was claimed. A change that quietly grew is a change
386	nobody agreed to, and it is the review that pays for it.
387	
388	Where the issue's scope turns out to be wrong rather than merely narrow — the fix is
389	impossible inside it — stop and say so. That is a finding, not an obstacle to route around.
390	
391	## 3. Do it
392	
393	**Ending in a diff:** write the change. Run whatever the project runs — tests, typecheck,
394	build — and run it because a claim is verified when it was observed, not when it was
395	expected.
396	
397	**Ending in evidence:** work the procedure the issue gives, in order. Where a step is
398	destructive or order-dependent, do not vary it. Capture as you go rather than
399	reconstructing afterwards:
400	
401	- the commands, exactly as run
402	- their output, verbatim
403	- the state before and after
404	- when, and by whom
405	
406	**Verify from outside the change.** Checking with the tool that made it proves the tool
407	ran, not that the world changed. A different vantage point is the whole value of the check.
408	
409	**Stop on a surprise.** A precondition that is false, an output that does not match, a step
410	that fails halfway — these end the run and go into the report. An operation abandoned
411	mid-procedure leaves the system in neither state, and the report is what tells someone.
412	
413	## 4. Record it
414	
415	**A diff:** commit to the claimed branch, citing the issue.
416	
417	The message carries **why**, not only what — the diff already shows what. Code says what it
418	does and tests say what it is for, but nothing except this message says why it was done this
419	way rather than the other way. When the code is deleted, its story goes with it and the
420	message is what survives.
421	
422	**Evidence:** put it on the issue, then close it — note first, close second, per step 0. The
423	issue is the only place this act is recorded, so the comment carries the commands, the
424	output and the before-and-after state, not a summary of them.
425	
426	**Do not close an issue that ends in a diff.** The change request closes it on merge, and
427	closing by hand strands the branch.
428	
429	## 5. Say what state it is in
430	
431	Not a verdict — a state, honestly named. The pass after this one routes on it, and it can
432	only route on the truth:
433	
434	| State | What it means |
435	|---|---|
436	| **done** | The acceptance line is satisfied, and you checked rather than assumed |
437	| **half done** | Real progress, the rest is clear and doable |
438	| **stuck** | Blocked on something you cannot resolve — say what, and who can |
439	| **more than one task** | This is two or more pieces of work wearing one issue number |
440	| **not started** | A precondition failed before anything was touched |
441	
442	**"Done" is the claim that costs most to get wrong**, because everything downstream trusts
443	it. Everything else is cheap to say and cheap to act on.
444	
445	## Noticing other issues
446	
447	While in here you will see issues that are already satisfied, stale, or done by something
448	else. **Say so; never close them.** An issue that looks done can be a false positive, and
449	closing one wrongly removes it from the board while the work stands undone.
450	
451	One line in the report: *"#38 looks already satisfied by <evidence>; close it?"* That is a
452	board tidied by work already happening, rather than a sweep nobody reaches for.
453	
454	## Steps
455	
456	Copy this checklist and tick each item as you finish it:
457	
458	    Task Progress:
459	    - [ ] Platform derived from the git remote, not assumed
460	    - [ ] Claim read — issue, comments, the stated reading, branch or no branch
461	    - [ ] Mode known: ends in a diff, or ends in evidence
462	    - [ ] Work done, and verified from outside itself
463	    - [ ] Recorded — committed with why, or evidence on the issue then closed
464	    - [ ] Scope held; anything found outside it reported, not absorbed
465	    - [ ] State named honestly, not graded
466	    - [ ] Other issues noticed along the way — offered, never closed
467	
468	## Report
469	
470	Two lines and a question:
471	
472	    HALF DONE — parser fixed and tested; the error message rewrite is untouched.
473	    Next: finish the message rewrite, ~20 min.
474	    Run it, or see what changed?
475	
476	An evidence run reports the same way, with what proves it:
477	
478	    DONE — cert rotated on staging, expiry now 2027-02-14, verified from an external probe.
479	    Next: nothing. #51 closed with the commands and output attached.
480	
481	A surprise is a state, and reads the same:
482	
483	    STUCK — the migration needs a maintenance window nobody has scheduled.
484	    Next: someone books the window, then this resumes from step 3.
485	
486	The two states easiest to leave unsaid, because neither feels like a result:
487	
488	    MORE THAN ONE TASK — #47 is a schema change and a UI change; they ship separately.
489	    Next: split it, then take the schema half.
490	
491	    NOT STARTED — the staging database is already on 16, so the precondition is false.
492	    Next: someone confirms whether #52 is stale before anything runs.
493	
494	The diff, the commands, the output and the trace are prepared and held until asked.
495

---
name: do-task
description: |
  Does the work a claimed issue describes — writes and commits the change, or performs the
  act and captures the evidence that it happened. Holds the scope the issue set, records
  why in the commit message rather than only what, and ends by stating what state the work
  is actually in rather than declaring it done. The write half of an issue; something else
  judges whether it finished.
when_to_use: |
  Use once an issue is claimed and the work should start, whatever kind it is — "implement
  it", "fix it", "make the change", "go ahead", "do it". Code: "write the parser fix".
  Docs: "update that README". Environment: "run the staging upgrade". Operations: "rotate
  the cert now", "run the migration", "restart it". Reach for it after take-issue has
  claimed something, and when the user says do it on work already understood. Not for

# Take an issue

Target: $ARGUMENTS — an issue number, or empty to take the next one available.

**This claims, it does not build.** It ends with an issue assigned, a branch cut where one
is warranted, and a statement of what was understood. Nothing in the working tree changes,
and nothing is acted on — an operation issue is claimed here and performed elsewhere. That gap is
deliberate: it is the last cheap moment to catch a misreading, and reading an issue wrong
is the failure that survives every later review, because every later review checks the work
against the misreading.

**It is also the test of the issue.** An issue that cannot be started without asking a
question is thin, and here is the only place that is discoverable.

**The point is to make the platform pay off.** Every act below is a `gh` or `glab` call a
person could make themselves. The value is not having to remember which, not having to
notice the two CLIs disagree, and not having to assemble the issue, its comments and its
links by hand. Where this skill would add a step the platform does not need, it is wrong —
process invented on top of a tracker is a cost the tracker was supposed to remove.

## 0. Which platform

Derive it — `git remote get-url origin`. Only the verbs this skill needs:

| | GitHub — `gh` | GitLab — `glab` |
|---|---|---|
| read, with comments | `gh issue view <N> --comments` | `glab issue view <N> --comments` |
| frontier | `gh issue list --state open --label <ready> --search "no:assignee"` | `glab issue list --label <ready> --output json --jq '[.[] \| select(.assignees\|length==0)]'` |
| claim | `gh issue edit <N> --add-assignee @me` | `glab issue update <N> --assignee <username>` |
| move state | `gh issue edit <N> --add-label <in-progress> --remove-label <ready>` | `glab issue update <N> --label <in-progress> --unlabel <ready>` |

**Unassigned is not a flag on either.** `gh` reaches it through search syntax;
`glab` has no unassigned filter at all — `--not-assignee` takes a username, not a blank —
so it needs JSON and a filter expression. That asymmetry is why the frontier is worth
writing down once rather than improvising per run.

**Moving a state means removing the old label, not only adding the new one.** Both CLIs
can (`gh --remove-label`, `glab --unlabel`) and it is the easiest half to forget. An issue
carrying `ready` and `in-progress` at once keeps coming back in the frontier, so the next
run offers work somebody already took.

`@me` is documented on `gh issue edit --add-assignee` and on `glab issue list --assignee`.
`glab issue update` takes a username, so resolve it rather than assuming the shorthand
carries across.

## 1. Resolve the portal

**Given a number**, that is the portal. Take it even if something else looks more urgent —
choosing for the user is not this skill's job.

**Given nothing**, run the frontier: open, carrying the project's ready-to-pick-up label,
unassigned, and not blocked. First in that set wins.

**Blocked-ness is not equally knowable.** GitHub answers it natively. On a free GitLab the
blocking relation is a paid feature, so what is reachable is a link that records a relation
and gates nothing — read the linked issues and judge it yourself, and say that is what you
did. Reporting an unverified frontier as verified is worse than reporting a short one.

**Empty frontier is an answer.** Report it and stop. Do not widen the query until something
appears; a frontier that had to be relaxed to produce work is not a frontier.

## 2. Read it whole

Body, every comment, labels, linked issues. Comments are where an issue is amended, and an
issue read without them is read at the moment it was filed rather than as it stands.

**If the issue links a session log**, read the part it points at. A body has to compress;
the log is where the reasoning behind it survives, so it is the cheap way to recover intent
the issue could not carry.

**Do not open it whole.** It is raw JSONL — one record per line, megabytes of it, most of
which is tool output and harness bookkeeping. Reading it end to end spends the context the
work needs. Pull out what was said instead:

    python3 -c "
    import json,sys
    for l in open(sys.argv[1]):
        d=json.loads(l)
        if d.get('type') not in ('user','assistant'): continue
        c=(d.get('message') or {}).get('content')
        if isinstance(c,str): print(d['type'],':',c[:2000]); continue
        for b in (c or []):
            if b.get('type')=='text': print(d['type'],':',b['text'][:2000])
    " .sessions/<uuid>.jsonl

Narrow it further where the issue names a line range or a topic. **Search the log, do not
read it** — you are recovering one decision, not reconstructing a session.

**A session log is an accuracy aid, not a requirement.** Most issues will not have one, and
none of them is unpickable for lacking it. Say it was absent and proceed on what the issue
says. Refusing work because a record is missing would make the record more important than
the work, which is backwards.

## 3. Is it pickable

Refuse, and name the gap, when any of these is true:

| The issue | Why it is not pickable |
|---|---|
| has no acceptance line | Nothing says when it is done, so nothing can say it was done wrong |
| has an acceptance line nobody else could check | "Quality is acceptable" hands the judgment back to whoever wrote it |
| is blocked, and the blocker is open | The work would be redone |
| is assigned to someone else | Two people on one issue is worse than nobody. Assigned to **you** is not a refusal — that is resuming, and it is the common case |
| describes a symptom with no reproduction, and is a bug | The first act would be inventing one |

**Refusing costs one message. Guessing costs the whole change.** A guess made here is
invisible afterwards: the branch, the commits and the review all inherit it, and every one
of them checks the work against the guess rather than against the need.

**Offer the fix, do not just name the gap.** A refusal that ends at "this has no
acceptance line" leaves the user with the same problem plus a delay. Propose the line, and
on a yes write it to the issue and take it in the same turn — the tracker gets better and
the work starts, which is the whole point of standing between a person and the platform.

Where it is close, ask rather than refusing. "Done when says the report is clearer —
clearer measured how?" is one question and it makes the issue permanently better.

## 4. Claim it

**First: will this end in a diff?** Not every issue does. Code, docs and
infrastructure-as-code produce a patch; an operation — a certificate rotated, a job re-run,
data migrated — produces evidence and never touches the tree. The issue's kind usually says
which, and its template says how it closes.

**No diff, no branch.** A branch with nothing on it is noise, and deleting it later reads as
work abandoned. Where it is genuinely unclear, ask — one question is cheaper than a stray
branch or a missing one.

Then claim it. **Local first, so a failure costs nothing anyone else can see:**

    1. branch   ONLY if a diff is coming. issue-<N>-<slug>, cut from the default branch
                derived rather than assumed. Where the project declares its own pattern,
                that wins. Branch already there? Check it out — resuming is not an error.
    2. assign   to yourself
    3. label    move the state — new label on, old label off

If a later act fails, undo backwards: delete the branch if one was cut, unassign. A
half-claim is worse than none — a branch with no assignment reads as unclaimed work, and an
assignment with no branch reads as work in progress nobody can find, unless no branch was
ever meant to exist. Say which acts landed rather than reporting the claim as whole.

## 5. Say what you understood

The output is a reading, offered for correction:

- what this issue is asking for, in your words rather than its
- what "done" means, quoted from the acceptance line
- what you will not touch, from Out of scope
- where a log exists and disagrees with the issue — **the log wins on reasoning, the issue
  wins on scope**. With no log, the issue is the whole of it and nothing is missing

Then stop. The next act is somebody's decision, not this skill's.

## Steps

Copy this checklist and tick each item as you finish it:

    Task Progress:
    - [ ] Platform derived from the git remote, not assumed
    - [ ] Portal resolved — number in hand, or frontier reported empty
    - [ ] Issue read whole, comments included
    - [ ] Session log read if the issue links one — absent is normal, not a blocker
    - [ ] Pickable — or refused, with the gap named
    - [ ] Diff coming? decided, and the branch cut only if so
    - [ ] Assignee and state label set, old label removed
    - [ ] Reading stated, and stopped

## Report

Two lines and a question:

    TAKEN — #42, on issue-42-report-wall. Done when: a report reads in under 30 seconds.
    Next: implement it.
    Run it, or see what I understood?

A refusal is a verdict and reads the same way:

    NOT PICKABLE — #51 has no acceptance line; nothing says when it is done.
    Next: add one to #51, then take it again.

The reading, the frontier query and the session excerpt are prepared and held until asked.

# Plan the work

Target: $ARGUMENTS — the issue to split, or the work just discussed.

**Most work should not be split.** An issue with five steps is one issue. Splitting is for
work that holds more than one *deliverable* — pieces that ship separately, get reviewed
separately, or could be done by different people at the same time. Splitting anything else
buys ceremony and pays in issues nobody closes.

**The platform already groups things.** Epics, milestones, iterations, project boards — they
exist, they have views the team already reads, and a hand-rolled parent issue with child
links drifts from whatever the board actually says. Use what is there.

## 0. What this platform can actually do

Derive the host — `git remote get-url origin` — then note that **neither CLI gives a
complete decomposition primitive.** Check before promising a structure:

| | GitHub — `gh` | GitLab — `glab` |
|---|---|---|
| create a grouping | `gh project create` · milestone via `gh api` | `glab milestone create` |
| attach an issue | `gh issue create -m <milestone> -p <project>` | `glab issue create --milestone <m> --epic <id>` |
| parent / child | sub-issues via `gh api` only — no first-class verb | epic only, and epics are a **paid tier** |
| sprint | a Project iteration field | `glab iteration` is **read-only** |
| weak fallback | — | `--linked-issues` — records a relation, gates nothing |

**Say what you got.** On a free GitLab there is no epic to attach to and no CLI to make one;
the reachable grouping is a milestone. Reporting a milestone as an epic, or a relation as a
dependency, promises structure the platform will not keep.

## 1. Should this be split at all

**Split when** the pieces are independently deliverable — each could be reviewed, merged, or
performed without the others, and each is worth doing even if the rest is dropped.

**Do not split when:**

- The steps are sequential parts of one deliverable. A migration with five steps ships once.
- One piece is real work and the rest is under an hour. File the small ones or fold them in.
- The split is by *layer* rather than by outcome — "the backend part" and "the frontend
  part" of one feature usually ship together and reviewing them apart helps nobody.
- Nobody will work on the pieces in parallel. Then the split is bookkeeping.

**The test:** could someone close one child and leave the others open, and would the board
still make sense? If not, it is one issue.

## 2. Find what the project already uses

Look before proposing. `gh project list` / `glab milestone list` show what exists, and the
issues already carry the answer — an open milestone with issues on it is the project's
grouping whatever anyone says.

**Where the project uses nothing**, ask rather than choosing. Introducing a board is a
decision about how a team works, and it is not this unit's to make. A flat set of issues
with no grouping is a legitimate answer and often the right one.

## 3. Write the children

**File each child rather than writing it here.** A child is a full issue and gets the same
treatment as any other: the kind decided, the matching template filled, the duplicate search
run, an acceptance line a stranger could check. Reimplementing that inside this unit
produces five thinner issues than the same work filed one at a time, which is the opposite
of what a split is for.

- **One deliverable each.** If a child needs its own children, the split was at the wrong
  level.
- **Its kind picks its template**, and the children need not share one. A feature may split
  into code, a doc, and an operation to run afterwards — three kinds, three templates,
  three different acceptance tests.
- **Ordering is a fact, not a wish.** Where one child genuinely cannot start until another
  finishes, record it with whatever the platform offers, and say what that actually
  enforces — see step 0.
- **Every child links the parent's session log**, where one exists. The reasoning behind
  the split is exactly what a body compresses away, and a child picked up next week starts
  cold without it. One link, not a copy.
- **The parent keeps the why.** Children carry their own scope and acceptance; the reasoning
  that led to this split stays in one place rather than being copied five times.

## 4. Attach and report

Create the grouping if the project has one and it does not exist yet, attach every child,
and leave the parent issue pointing at them.

**Do not leave a half-plan.** Five children created and two attached is worse than none —
the board shows a structure that is not there. If attachment fails partway, say which
landed.

## Steps

Copy this checklist and tick each item as you finish it:

    Task Progress:
    - [ ] Platform derived, and its actual grouping support checked
    - [ ] Splitting justified — pieces are independently deliverable
    - [ ] Existing grouping found, or asked for; none is a valid answer
    - [ ] Children written as full issues, each with one deliverable
    - [ ] Ordering recorded, and what it enforces stated honestly
    - [ ] Every child attached, or the partial state reported

## Report

Two lines and a question:

    SPLIT — #47 into #48, #49, #50 on milestone "parser rewrite". #49 waits on #48.
    Next: take #48 — the other two are blocked until it lands.
    Run it, or see the children?

Declining to split is the more common outcome and reads the same:

    NOT SPLIT — #47 is five steps of one migration; it ships once.
    Next: take #47 as it stands.

Where the platform could not carry the structure, that belongs in the first line:

    SPLIT — #47 into #48, #49, #50 on milestone "parser rewrite". No epic: this
    instance has none, and the ordering is a relation that gates nothing.
    Next: take #48, and do not rely on the platform to stop #49 starting early.

The children, the grouping, and the trace are prepared and held until asked.

# Do the task

Target: $ARGUMENTS — the claimed issue, or the one just picked up.

**This writes; it does not judge.** It ends with a commit or a captured act, and a plain
statement of what state the work is in. Deciding whether that state is *done* belongs to
the pass after this one — an author grading their own work grades it done, which is why the
grading is somebody else's.

**Two modes, and the issue already says which.** Work ending in a diff writes files and
commits them. Work ending in evidence performs an act and records that it happened. A
certificate rotation produces no patch; the record of the commands and their output is the
only proof it occurred.

## 0. Which platform

Derive it — `git remote get-url origin`. Only the verbs this skill needs:

| | GitHub — `gh` | GitLab — `glab` |
|---|---|---|
| comment | `gh issue comment <N> --body "…"` | `glab issue note <N> -m "…"` |
| close with evidence | `gh issue close <N> --comment "…"` | **two commands** — `glab issue note <N> -m "…"` then `glab issue close <N>` |

**`glab issue close` takes no comment.** Note first, close second. Reversed, a failed note
leaves a closed issue with no record of what was done — and a closed issue is the one nobody
looks at again.

## 1. Know what you are doing

Read the claim before touching anything: the issue, its comments, the reading `take-issue`
stated, and the branch — or the absence of one, which means this ends in evidence.

**No claim to read?** "Just fix it" is what people actually type, and it arrives with no
assignee, no stated reading, and often no issue. That is workable, not an error — say which
you have and carry on:

| What is missing | What to do |
|---|---|
| the branch | Decide the mode yourself: does this end in a diff or in evidence? |
| the stated reading | Read the issue and state your own before starting. It is the cheap moment |
| the issue itself | Do the work if it is small. If it is not, say so — untracked work of any size is invisible the moment this session ends |

Never invent a claim. Reporting an issue as claimed when nothing on the platform says so is
worse than working without one.

**Three sources, three authorities.** They disagree more often than anyone expects:

| Source | Binds on |
|---|---|
| the code | **reality** — what is true now, whatever anything says |
| the issue | **scope** — what this change may touch |
| the log | **nothing.** It informs |

A log that seems to forbid something is not a constraint; it is a previous person's
situation, recorded under conditions that may no longer hold. Where the issue and the code
disagree about what exists, the code is right and the issue needs a comment.

## 2. Hold the scope

**`Out of scope` is binding.** It is the one section written specifically to stop the next
person widening the work, and that next person is now you.

Finding something else worth doing is normal and is not permission. File it, or say it in
the report, and carry on with what was claimed. A change that quietly grew is a change
nobody agreed to, and it is the review that pays for it.

Where the issue's scope turns out to be wrong rather than merely narrow — the fix is
impossible inside it — stop and say so. That is a finding, not an obstacle to route around.

## 3. Do it

**Ending in a diff:** write the change. Run whatever the project runs — tests, typecheck,
build — and run it because a claim is verified when it was observed, not when it was
expected.

**Ending in evidence:** work the procedure the issue gives, in order. Where a step is
destructive or order-dependent, do not vary it. Capture as you go rather than
reconstructing afterwards:

- the commands, exactly as run
- their output, verbatim
- the state before and after
- when, and by whom

**Verify from outside the change.** Checking with the tool that made it proves the tool
ran, not that the world changed. A different vantage point is the whole value of the check.

**Stop on a surprise.** A precondition that is false, an output that does not match, a step
that fails halfway — these end the run and go into the report. An operation abandoned
mid-procedure leaves the system in neither state, and the report is what tells someone.

## 4. Record it

**A diff:** commit to the claimed branch, citing the issue.

The message carries **why**, not only what — the diff already shows what. Code says what it
does and tests say what it is for, but nothing except this message says why it was done this
way rather than the other way. When the code is deleted, its story goes with it and the
message is what survives.

**Evidence:** put it on the issue, then close it — note first, close second, per step 0. The
issue is the only place this act is recorded, so the comment carries the commands, the
output and the before-and-after state, not a summary of them.

**Do not close an issue that ends in a diff.** The change request closes it on merge, and
closing by hand strands the branch.

## 5. Say what state it is in

Not a verdict — a state, honestly named. The pass after this one routes on it, and it can
only route on the truth:

| State | What it means |
|---|---|
| **done** | The acceptance line is satisfied, and you checked rather than assumed |
| **half done** | Real progress, the rest is clear and doable |
| **stuck** | Blocked on something you cannot resolve — say what, and who can |
| **more than one task** | This is two or more pieces of work wearing one issue number |
| **not started** | A precondition failed before anything was touched |

**"Done" is the claim that costs most to get wrong**, because everything downstream trusts
it. Everything else is cheap to say and cheap to act on.

## Noticing other issues

While in here you will see issues that are already satisfied, stale, or done by something
else. **Say so; never close them.** An issue that looks done can be a false positive, and
closing one wrongly removes it from the board while the work stands undone.

One line in the report: *"#38 looks already satisfied by <evidence>; close it?"* That is a
board tidied by work already happening, rather than a sweep nobody reaches for.

## Steps

Copy this checklist and tick each item as you finish it:

    Task Progress:
    - [ ] Platform derived from the git remote, not assumed
    - [ ] Claim read — issue, comments, the stated reading, branch or no branch
    - [ ] Mode known: ends in a diff, or ends in evidence
    - [ ] Work done, and verified from outside itself
    - [ ] Recorded — committed with why, or evidence on the issue then closed
    - [ ] Scope held; anything found outside it reported, not absorbed
    - [ ] State named honestly, not graded
    - [ ] Other issues noticed along the way — offered, never closed

## Report

Two lines and a question:

    HALF DONE — parser fixed and tested; the error message rewrite is untouched.
    Next: finish the message rewrite, ~20 min.
    Run it, or see what changed?

An evidence run reports the same way, with what proves it:

    DONE — cert rotated on staging, expiry now 2027-02-14, verified from an external probe.
    Next: nothing. #51 closed with the commands and output attached.

A surprise is a state, and reads the same:

    STUCK — the migration needs a maintenance window nobody has scheduled.
    Next: someone books the window, then this resumes from step 3.

The two states easiest to leave unsaid, because neither feels like a result:

    MORE THAN ONE TASK — #47 is a schema change and a UI change; they ship separately.
    Next: split it, then take the schema half.

    NOT STARTED — the staging database is already on 16, so the precondition is false.
    Next: someone confirms whether #52 is stale before anything runs.

The diff, the commands, the output and the trace are prepared and held until asked.

The main idea of the combined `do-task` is **carrying one tracked issue from claim to a named state, while holding it to its scope.**

The sections line up under that idea in three stages:

1. **Take:** read the issue whole, refuse it if nobody else could check its acceptance line, then claim it. It creates a branch only if a code change is coming.
2. **Plan:** split the issue only when its pieces ship separately. Most work stays one issue.
3. **Do:** make the change or perform the act, keep to the issue's scope, record it (a commit with the reason, or evidence on the issue), and name its state honestly.

The same rule runs through all three: **the agent works on the platform and never grades its own work.** The code decides what's true now, the issue sets the scope, and the session log only informs.

Joining the three files left these conflicts in their text:
- **Each stage still ends in "stop".** Take says "Then stop. The next act is somebody's decision", and Plan and Do each end with their own report. As one skill, it stops twice before the actual work.
- **The frontmatter describes only the third stage.** It says "Not for choosing what to work on", but the Take stage picks the next issue when none is named.
- **The same steps appear more than once:** "Which platform" is written out twice, there are three checklists, and there are three report formats.

The full structure study, one list item per section with each clause's subject in bold and its action in a code span, is at `scratchpad/do-task-structure.md`.

-  is actually in rather than declaring it done. The write half of an issue; something else

-  it", "fix it", "make the change", "go ahead", "do it". Code: "write the parser fix".
-  Docs: "update that README". Environment: "run the staging upgrade". Operations: "rotate
-  the cert now", "run the migration", "restart it". Reach for it after take-issue has

-# Take an issue
-Target: $ARGUMENTS — an issue number, or empty to take the next one available.
-**This claims, it does not build.** It ends with an issue assigned, a branch cut where one
-is warranted, and a statement of what was understood. Nothing in the working tree changes,
-and nothing is acted on — an operation issue is claimed here and performed elsewhere. That gap is
-deliberate: it is the last cheap moment to catch a misreading, and reading an issue wrong
-is the failure that survives every later review, because every later review checks the work
-against the misreading.
-**It is also the test of the issue.** An issue that cannot be started without asking a
-question is thin, and here is the only place that is discoverable.
-**The point is to make the platform pay off.** Every act below is a `gh` or `glab` call a
-person could make themselves. The value is not having to remember which, not having to
-notice the two CLIs disagree, and not having to assemble the issue, its comments and its
-links by hand. Where this skill would add a step the platform does not need, it is wrong —
-process invented on top of a tracker is a cost the tracker was supposed to remove.
-## 0. Which platform
-Derive it — `git remote get-url origin`. Only the verbs this skill needs:
-| | GitHub — `gh` | GitLab — `glab` |
-| read, with comments | `gh issue view <N> --comments` | `glab issue view <N> --comments` |
-| frontier | `gh issue list --state open --label <ready> --search "no:assignee"` | `glab issue list --label <ready> --output json --jq '[.[] \| select(.assignees\|length==0)]'` |
-| claim | `gh issue edit <N> --add-assignee @me` | `glab issue update <N> --assignee <username>` |
-| move state | `gh issue edit <N> --add-label <in-progress> --remove-label <ready>` | `glab issue update <N> --label <in-progress> --unlabel <ready>` |
-**Unassigned is not a flag on either.** `gh` reaches it through search syntax;
-`glab` has no unassigned filter at all — `--not-assignee` takes a username, not a blank —
-so it needs JSON and a filter expression. That asymmetry is why the frontier is worth
-writing down once rather than improvising per run.
-**Moving a state means removing the old label, not only adding the new one.** Both CLIs
-can (`gh --remove-label`, `glab --unlabel`) and it is the easiest half to forget. An issue
-carrying `ready` and `in-progress` at once keeps coming back in the frontier, so the next
-run offers work somebody already took.
-`@me` is documented on `gh issue edit --add-assignee` and on `glab issue list --assignee`.
-`glab issue update` takes a username, so resolve it rather than assuming the shorthand
-carries across.
-## 1. Resolve the portal
-**Given a number**, that is the portal. Take it even if something else looks more urgent —
-choosing for the user is not this skill's job.
-**Given nothing**, run the frontier: open, carrying the project's ready-to-pick-up label,
-unassigned, and not blocked. First in that set wins.
-**Blocked-ness is not equally knowable.** GitHub answers it natively. On a free GitLab the
-blocking relation is a paid feature, so what is reachable is a link that records a relation
-and gates nothing — read the linked issues and judge it yourself, and say that is what you
-did. Reporting an unverified frontier as verified is worse than reporting a short one.
-**Empty frontier is an answer.** Report it and stop. Do not widen the query until something
-appears; a frontier that had to be relaxed to produce work is not a frontier.
-## 2. Read it whole
-Body, every comment, labels, linked issues. Comments are where an issue is amended, and an
-issue read without them is read at the moment it was filed rather than as it stands.
-**If the issue links a session log**, read the part it points at. A body has to compress;
-the log is where the reasoning behind it survives, so it is the cheap way to recover intent
-the issue could not carry.
-**Do not open it whole.** It is raw JSONL — one record per line, megabytes of it, most of
-which is tool output and harness bookkeeping. Reading it end to end spends the context the
-work needs. Pull out what was said instead:
-    python3 -c "
-    import json,sys
-    for l in open(sys.argv[1]):
-        d=json.loads(l)
-        if d.get('type') not in ('user','assistant'): continue
-        c=(d.get('message') or {}).get('content')
-        if isinstance(c,str): print(d['type'],':',c[:2000]); continue
-        for b in (c or []):
-            if b.get('type')=='text': print(d['type'],':',b['text'][:2000])
-    " .sessions/<uuid>.jsonl
-Narrow it further where the issue names a line range or a topic. **Search the log, do not
-read it** — you are recovering one decision, not reconstructing a session.
-**A session log is an accuracy aid, not a requirement.** Most issues will not have one, and
-none of them is unpickable for lacking it. Say it was absent and proceed on what the issue
-says. Refusing work because a record is missing would make the record more important than
-the work, which is backwards.
-## 3. Is it pickable
-Refuse, and name the gap, when any of these is true:
-| The issue | Why it is not pickable |
-| has no acceptance line | Nothing says when it is done, so nothing can say it was done wrong |
-| has an acceptance line nobody else could check | "Quality is acceptable" hands the judgment back to whoever wrote it |
-| is blocked, and the blocker is open | The work would be redone |
-| is assigned to someone else | Two people on one issue is worse than nobody. Assigned to **you** is not a refusal — that is resuming, and it is the common case |
-| describes a symptom with no reproduction, and is a bug | The first act would be inventing one |
-**Refusing costs one message. Guessing costs the whole change.** A guess made here is
-invisible afterwards: the branch, the commits and the review all inherit it, and every one
-of them checks the work against the guess rather than against the need.
-**Offer the fix, do not just name the gap.** A refusal that ends at "this has no
-acceptance line" leaves the user with the same problem plus a delay. Propose the line, and
-on a yes write it to the issue and take it in the same turn — the tracker gets better and
-the work starts, which is the whole point of standing between a person and the platform.
-Where it is close, ask rather than refusing. "Done when says the report is clearer —
-clearer measured how?" is one question and it makes the issue permanently better.
-## 4. Claim it
-**First: will this end in a diff?** Not every issue does. Code, docs and
-infrastructure-as-code produce a patch; an operation — a certificate rotated, a job re-run,
-data migrated — produces evidence and never touches the tree. The issue's kind usually says
-which, and its template says how it closes.
-**No diff, no branch.** A branch with nothing on it is noise, and deleting it later reads as
-work abandoned. Where it is genuinely unclear, ask — one question is cheaper than a stray
-branch or a missing one.
-Then claim it. **Local first, so a failure costs nothing anyone else can see:**
-    1. branch   ONLY if a diff is coming. issue-<N>-<slug>, cut from the default branch
-                derived rather than assumed. Where the project declares its own pattern,
-                that wins. Branch already there? Check it out — resuming is not an error.
-    2. assign   to yourself
-    3. label    move the state — new label on, old label off

-assignment with no branch reads as work in progress nobody can find, unless no branch was
-ever meant to exist. Say which acts landed rather than reporting the claim as whole.
-## 5. Say what you understood
-The output is a reading, offered for correction:
-- what this issue is asking for, in your words rather than its
-- what "done" means, quoted from the acceptance line
-- what you will not touch, from Out of scope
-- where a log exists and disagrees with the issue — **the log wins on reasoning, the issue
-  wins on scope**. With no log, the issue is the whole of it and nothing is missing

-    Task Progress:
-    - [ ] Platform derived from the git remote, not assumed
-    - [ ] Portal resolved — number in hand, or frontier reported empty

-    - [ ] Session log read if the issue links one — absent is normal, not a blocker

-    Next: implement it.
-    Run it, or see what I understood?
-A refusal is a verdict and reads the same way:
-    NOT PICKABLE — #51 has no acceptance line; nothing says when it is done.

-| close with evidence | `gh issue close <N> --comment "…"` | **two commands** — `glab issue note <N> -m "…"` then `glab issue close <N>` |
-**`glab issue close` takes no comment.** Note first, close second. Reversed, a failed note
-leaves a closed issue with no record of what was done — and a closed issue is the one nobody
-looks at again.
-## 1. Know what you are doing
-Read the claim before touching anything: the issue, its comments, the reading `take-issue`
-stated, and the branch — or the absence of one, which means this ends in evidence.
-**No claim to read?** "Just fix it" is what people actually type, and it arrives with no
-assignee, no stated reading, and often no issue. That is workable, not an error — say which
-you have and carry on:
-| What is missing | What to do |
-| the branch | Decide the mode yourself: does this end in a diff or in evidence? |
-| the stated reading | Read the issue and state your own before starting. It is the cheap moment |
-| the issue itself | Do the work if it is small. If it is not, say so — untracked work of any size is invisible the moment this session ends |
-Never invent a claim. Reporting an issue as claimed when nothing on the platform says so is
-worse than working without one.
-**Three sources, three authorities.** They disagree more often than anyone expects:
-| Source | Binds on |
-| the code | **reality** — what is true now, whatever anything says |
-| the issue | **scope** — what this change may touch |
-| the log | **nothing.** It informs |
-A log that seems to forbid something is not a constraint; it is a previous person's
-situation, recorded under conditions that may no longer hold. Where the issue and the code
-disagree about what exists, the code is right and the issue needs a comment.
-## 2. Hold the scope
-**`Out of scope` is binding.** It is the one section written specifically to stop the next
-person widening the work, and that next person is now you.
-Finding something else worth doing is normal and is not permission. File it, or say it in
-the report, and carry on with what was claimed. A change that quietly grew is a change
-nobody agreed to, and it is the review that pays for it.
-Where the issue's scope turns out to be wrong rather than merely narrow — the fix is
-impossible inside it — stop and say so. That is a finding, not an obstacle to route around.
-## 3. Do it
-**Ending in a diff:** write the change. Run whatever the project runs — tests, typecheck,
-build — and run it because a claim is verified when it was observed, not when it was
-expected.
-**Ending in evidence:** work the procedure the issue gives, in order. Where a step is
-destructive or order-dependent, do not vary it. Capture as you go rather than
-reconstructing afterwards:
-- the commands, exactly as run
-- their output, verbatim
-- the state before and after
-- when, and by whom
-**Verify from outside the change.** Checking with the tool that made it proves the tool
-ran, not that the world changed. A different vantage point is the whole value of the check.
-**Stop on a surprise.** A precondition that is false, an output that does not match, a step
-that fails halfway — these end the run and go into the report. An operation abandoned
-mid-procedure leaves the system in neither state, and the report is what tells someone.
-## 4. Record it
-**A diff:** commit to the claimed branch, citing the issue.
-The message carries **why**, not only what — the diff already shows what. Code says what it
-does and tests say what it is for, but nothing except this message says why it was done this
-way rather than the other way. When the code is deleted, its story goes with it and the
-message is what survives.
-**Evidence:** put it on the issue, then close it — note first, close second, per step 0. The
-issue is the only place this act is recorded, so the comment carries the commands, the
-output and the before-and-after state, not a summary of them.
-**Do not close an issue that ends in a diff.** The change request closes it on merge, and
-closing by hand strands the branch.
-## 5. Say what state it is in
-Not a verdict — a state, honestly named. The pass after this one routes on it, and it can
-only route on the truth:
-| State | What it means |
-| **done** | The acceptance line is satisfied, and you checked rather than assumed |
-| **half done** | Real progress, the rest is clear and doable |
-| **stuck** | Blocked on something you cannot resolve — say what, and who can |
-| **more than one task** | This is two or more pieces of work wearing one issue number |
-| **not started** | A precondition failed before anything was touched |
-**"Done" is the claim that costs most to get wrong**, because everything downstream trusts
-it. Everything else is cheap to say and cheap to act on.
-## Noticing other issues
-While in here you will see issues that are already satisfied, stale, or done by something
-else. **Say so; never close them.** An issue that looks done can be a false positive, and
-closing one wrongly removes it from the board while the work stands undone.
-One line in the report: *"#38 looks already satisfied by <evidence>; close it?"* That is a
-board tidied by work already happening, rather than a sweep nobody reaches for.
-## Steps
-Copy this checklist and tick each item as you finish it:
-    Task Progress:
-    - [ ] Platform derived from the git remote, not assumed
-    - [ ] Claim read — issue, comments, the stated reading, branch or no branch
-    - [ ] Mode known: ends in a diff, or ends in evidence
-    - [ ] Work done, and verified from outside itself
-    - [ ] Recorded — committed with why, or evidence on the issue then closed
-    - [ ] Scope held; anything found outside it reported, not absorbed
-    - [ ] State named honestly, not graded
-    - [ ] Other issues noticed along the way — offered, never closed
-## Report
-Two lines and a question:
-    HALF DONE — parser fixed and tested; the error message rewrite is untouched.
-    Next: finish the message rewrite, ~20 min.
-    Run it, or see what changed?
-An evidence run reports the same way, with what proves it:
-    DONE — cert rotated on staging, expiry now 2027-02-14, verified from an external probe.
-    Next: nothing. #51 closed with the commands and output attached.
-A surprise is a state, and reads the same:
-    STUCK — the migration needs a maintenance window nobody has scheduled.
-    Next: someone books the window, then this resumes from step 3.
-The two states easiest to leave unsaid, because neither feels like a result:
-    MORE THAN ONE TASK — #47 is a schema change and a UI change; they ship separately.
-    Next: split it, then take the schema half.
-    NOT STARTED — the staging database is already on 16, so the precondition is false.
-    Next: someone confirms whether #52 is stale before anything runs.
-The diff, the commands, the output and the trace are prepared and held until asked.

```
Work an issue:

```

I agree for most of them. The test I'd use is whether the agent would skip the step without being told. The description names three failures: starting before reading the whole issue, going past the scope, and grading its own work as done. Only three steps answer those:

- **1. Read the issue, its comments and any session log it links.** This answers "starts before it reads the issue whole."
- **5. Touch nothing the issue puts out of scope.** This answers "widen past its scope."
- **9. Report the state instead of "done".** This answers "graded done by the agent that wrote it."

The rest are normal process that any agent does anyway: assign, branch, do the work, verify, commit.

Two are on the edge:
- **2. Split:** agents rarely split without being told, but it rarely comes up. Leaving it out costs little.
- **6. Stop when surprised:** agents do tend to push past a failed precondition. The description doesn't mention it, though, so keeping it would mean adding a fourth failure there.

My recommendation is to keep 1, 5 and 9, reworded to stand on their own:

```
Work an issue:
1. Read the issue, its comments and any session log it links.
2. Touch nothing the issue puts out of scope.
3. Report the state: done, half done, stuck, more than one task, or not started.
```

name: file-issue
description: |

  else can check. Creates the portal every later step resolves back to.
when_to_use: |
  Use whenever work is identified but not started, of any kind — not only code. Code:
  "this is broken", "raise a bug", "we should track this", "someone should fix that".
  Docs: "the README is wrong", "nobody can find how to run this", "that page is stale",
  "this needs writing up". Environment: "staging is on the old version", "we should
  upgrade that", "this config drifted", "we need a bigger instance". Operations: "the cert
  expires next week", "someone has to rotate that key", "we need to migrate the data",
  "that job needs re-running". Also the generic ones: "file an issue", "that's a separate
  problem", "let's do that later", "add it to the backlog". Reach for it when a session
  surfaces a second problem while working on a first, which is the case that most often
  goes unrecorded, and when the thing is an act to perform rather than code to write. Not
  for a question, a thing already underway, or a fix smaller than the issue describing it.
argument-hint: "[what to file]"
---

# File an issue

Target: $ARGUMENTS — what to file, or the thing just discussed.

**The issue is a portal, not a record.** Everything after it resolves backwards through
it: a branch takes its name, a commit cites it, a PR closes it, and an agent picking up
cold reads it first. What it cannot do is carry the reasoning that produced it — an issue
body is a summary by nature, and summarising is where the intent shifts.

So the split is: **the issue states the decision and the test; the session log holds the
reasoning.** The issue links to the log rather than absorbing it.

**The point is to make the platform pay off.** Every act below is a `gh` or `glab` call a
person could make themselves. The value is not having to remember which, not having to
notice the two CLIs disagree, and not having to write a body that a stranger can act on
from a standing start. Where this skill would add a step the platform does not need, it is
wrong — process invented on top of a tracker is a cost the tracker was supposed to remove.

## 0. Which platform

**Derive it, never assume it.** `git remote get-url origin` names the host. No address
belongs in this file: one a person has to keep correct goes stale silently.

| | GitHub — `gh` | GitLab — `glab` |
|---|---|---|
| create | `gh issue create --body-file <f>` | `glab issue create -d "$(cat <f>)"` — there is no `--body-file` |
| search | `gh issue list --search "…" --state all` | `glab issue list --search "…" --in title,description --all` |
| comment | `gh issue comment` | `glab issue note` |
| label | `gh issue edit --add-label` | `glab issue update --label` |
| change request | `pr` | `mr` |
| templates live in | `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/` | `.gitlab/issue_templates/`, reachable as `--template <name>` |

Both read the repository from the git remote, so neither takes a `--repo` argument from
inside the clone.

**Linking differs, and it is the one place to stop and say so.** GitHub carries dependencies
natively. GitLab's blocking relationships are a paid tier; on a free instance the reachable
verb is `--linked-issues` with `--link-type relates_to`, which records a relation but does
not gate anything. Say which you got — a relation reported as a dependency is a promise the
platform will not keep.

## 1. Should this be an issue at all

The judgment the whole workflow rests on. File too eagerly and the tracker fills with
things nobody closes; too reluctantly and the work happens with no record.

**Do not file:**

- A question the reply answers.
- A fix smaller than the issue describing it. A typo takes ten seconds; the issue takes
  two minutes and a close.
- Thinking aloud, exploring an idea, weighing an approach. A decision is not yet made.

## 5. Create it, and say where it went

    gh   issue create --title "<states the problem, not the fix>" --body-file <f>
    glab issue create --title "<states the problem, not the fix>" -d "$(cat <f>)"

Then set whatever label marks *ready to be picked up* in this project. Where the project
declares none, say so rather than inventing one.

Blocked by something? Record it as a real edge where the platform has them, and report
what you actually got — see step 0.

## Steps

Copy this checklist and tick each item as you finish it:

    Task Progress:
    - [ ] Platform derived from the git remote, not assumed
    - [ ] Decided it needs tracking — and said why, if it was close
    - [ ] Searched for an existing issue
    - [ ] Session saved and linked, or its absence accepted and Context omitted
    - [ ] Template picked — bug · task · docs · environment · operation
    - [ ] Issue created, labelled; linking reported as what the platform gave
    - [ ] Verdict reported

## Report

Two lines and a question:

    FILED — #42, blocked by #38, log at .sessions/<uuid>.jsonl
    Next: nothing. It is pickable when #38 closes.
    Want the body?

When it was decided *not* to file, that is still a verdict and still needs saying:

    NOT FILED — a typo fix, already done in this session.
    Next: nothing.

And when it should be filed but was not — the body is written and creation was deferred,
usually because someone asked for it that way:

    DRAFTED — body written to <path>, not on the platform.
    Next: create it, or say what to change first.

**Say which of the three it was.** A draft reported as filed is the worst of them: the work
looks tracked and nothing is.

The body, the search results and the session path are prepared and held until asked.

content.text:
Most of `file-issue` is standard issue hygiene: search for duplicates first, use templates, give clear titles, add labels. Here's where it departs from common practice, most unusual first:

1. **It commits the raw session log to the repo.** Common practice is to summarize the discussion in the issue or link to a chat. This skill copies the agent's full `.jsonl` transcript into `.sessions/` and commits it: raw, whole, unedited. It rejects even a Markdown rendering, as a filter that drops content. The issue links to the log instead of absorbing it. The log is still optional: if there isn't one, the issue is filed anyway.

2. **It quotes the request instead of paraphrasing it.** The usual habit is to rewrite the ask into clean tracker language, like "Improve report formatting". This skill puts the user's own words in the `What` section, because paraphrasing is where intent first drifts.

3. **It treats the issue as a portal, not a record.** Usually an issue is a ticket that describes the work. Here, every later step resolves back through the issue: the branch name, the commit, the PR closing it, and a cold agent picking it up.

4. **It decides whether to file at all.** Common practice leans toward "put it in the backlog". This skill refuses to file a question, a fix smaller than its issue (a typo), or thinking aloud. It pushes hardest on the case teams usually drop: a second problem found while working on the first.

5. **Issue kinds follow how the work ends, not just bug versus feature.** It has five templates, including **operation** and **environment** for work that isn't code. Each kind states whether it ends in a diff (closed by merging a PR) or in evidence (closed by hand with commands and output attached).

6. **"Done when" is required and must be checkable by someone else.** Usually acceptance criteria are optional or vague. Here, if you can't write a line a stranger could check, the thing isn't ready to be an issue.

7. **An agent must meet a higher bar than a person.** A bug filed by an agent must include **Root cause** and **Proposed fix**: eight required sections, which is deliberately more than the usual guidance of five or six. The reasoning is that an agent has just watched the failure happen.

8. **"Out of scope" does real work.** It's often skipped. Here it records a decision, so later work can't quietly widen.

9. **The project's own templates win, and the skill places its templates into the repo.** That way, filing through the web form and through the CLI give the same sections.

Items 1, 2, 4 and 6 are what make this skill different. Items 3 and 9 are about how it fits the workflow. The `gh` versus `glab` command table is ordinary reference that an agent already knows.

-So the split is: **the issue states the decision and the test; the session log holds the
-reasoning.** The issue links to the log rather than absorbing it.
-**The point is to make the platform pay off.** Every act below is a `gh` or `glab` call a
-person could make themselves. The value is not having to remember which, not having to
-notice the two CLIs disagree, and not having to write a body that a stranger can act on

-wrong — process invented on top of a tracker is a cost the tracker was supposed to remove.
-## 0. Which platform
-**Derive it, never assume it.** `git remote get-url origin` names the host. No address
-belongs in this file: one a person has to keep correct goes stale silently.
-| | GitHub — `gh` | GitLab — `glab` |
-| create | `gh issue create --body-file <f>` | `glab issue create -d "$(cat <f>)"` — there is no `--body-file` |
-| search | `gh issue list --search "…" --state all` | `glab issue list --search "…" --in title,description --all` |
-| comment | `gh issue comment` | `glab issue note` |
-| label | `gh issue edit --add-label` | `glab issue update --label` |
-| change request | `pr` | `mr` |
-| templates live in | `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/` | `.gitlab/issue_templates/`, reachable as `--template <name>` |
-Both read the repository from the git remote, so neither takes a `--repo` argument from
-inside the clone.
-**Linking differs, and it is the one place to stop and say so.** GitHub carries dependencies
-natively. GitLab's blocking relationships are a paid tier; on a free instance the reachable
-verb is `--linked-issues` with `--link-type relates_to`, which records a relation but does
-not gate anything. Say which you got — a relation reported as a dependency is a promise the
-platform will not keep.
-## 1. Should this be an issue at all

-things nobody closes; too reluctantly and the work happens with no record.
-**Do not file:**
-- A question the reply answers.
-- A fix smaller than the issue describing it. A typo takes ten seconds; the issue takes
-  two minutes and a close.
-- Thinking aloud, exploring an idea, weighing an approach. A decision is not yet made.
-- Something already being done in this session and about to be committed.
-**Do file:**
-- A second problem surfaced while working on a first. **This is the case that goes
-  unrecorded most often** — the session ends and the observation dies with it.
-- Anything that will be picked up by someone, or something, other than this session.
-- A decision made here that later work must not silently reverse.
-**Uncertain? Ask.** A user who says "we should probably…" has not decided. One question is
-cheaper than an issue nobody wanted.
-## 2. Search before creating
